strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: bringing high-resolution 3D generation into a unified MLLM framework rather than relying only on external 3D generators or low-resolution symbolic/voxel proxies.

The proposed TokenAR/BlockAR mixture-of-transformers design is a plausible architectural response to the long-sequence nature of 3D latents, and the manuscript gives a clear high-level explanation of how text, image, and 3D tokens are routed through the system.

The experiments show encouraging results among MLLM-based 3D generation baselines: the method improves over SAR3D and ShapeLLM-Omni on p-FID/p-KID and several perceptual/CLIP metrics, and the qualitative examples suggest better geometric completeness than those MLLM baselines.
The ablations are useful: stronger VAE, MoT, larger backbone, and longer 3D token budgets all improve p-FID/p-KID, supporting several of the main design choices.
The authors include some limitations and failure cases, including semantic hallucination and the gap to leading commercial/non-MLLM 3D generation systems.
weaknesses: The central claim of high-resolution, end-to-end 3D generation inside an MLLM is only partially supported. The model depends heavily on a frozen Hunyuan3D-2.1 VAE and material generator, and the paper does not sufficiently disentangle what is learned by CG-MLLM from what is inherited from this strong pretrained 3D generator/representation.

The comparison is incomplete for the strongest claim. The method is best only among MLLM-based models, while TRELLIS substantially outperforms it on p-FID/p-KID and SAM3D/Hunyuan3D are competitive or better on several other metrics. The abstract and introduction overstate the result as significantly outperforming existing MLLMs/high-fidelity 3D systems without consistently qualifying the scope.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper omits key training details such as dataset sizes after filtering, training steps/epochs, batch construction, model parameter counts for TokenAR/BlockAR, exact prompts, preprocessing scripts, evaluation protocol details, and whether code/model/data splits will be released.

The user study is under-specified: it mentions 100 questionnaires and about 2,400 data points, but does not describe participant recruitment, randomization, rating scale, statistical tests, prompts, blinding, or confidence intervals. This makes the reported preference score hard to interpret.

The 3D understanding claim is not fully convincing. The captioning evaluation compares image-input CG-MLLM against image VLMs and separately against 3D-latent-input models, but the dataset captions are acknowledged to be short and MLLM-generated. The apparent improvement over Qwen3-VL may reflect training distribution or caption style rather than robust 3D spatial reasoning.

Several metrics are only loosely connected to actual 3D asset quality. CLIP, MUSIQ, and CLIP-IQA are image-space or perceptual proxies; p-FID/p-KID details are not described enough to know what renderings/features are used. There is little evaluation of topology, mesh validity, physical plausibility, texture fidelity, or multi-view consistency.

Presentation is generally readable but sometimes imprecise and overly broad, with AGI motivation, 'true spatial intelligence', and 'physical consistency' claims that are not demonstrated. Some sections read like background exposition rather than method detail.

Ethics/impact discussion is boilerplate and inadequate for generative 3D assets. The paper should discuss potential misuse, dataset licensing/consent issues around Objaverse-style assets, watermarking/provenance, and impacts on 3D content creators.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: bringing 3D generation and 3D-related captioning into a unified multimodal LLM framework rather than treating 3D synthesis as a fully separate module.

The proposed system is reasonably coherent at a high level, combining a Qwen3-VL-style backbone, a Hunyuan3D VAE latent space, and separate TokenAR/BlockAR transformers for sequential and block-level generation.

The authors include comparisons against both MLLM-based and non-MLLM 3D generators, report several automatic metrics plus a user study, and provide some ablations on VAE choice, MoT usage, backbone scale, and token budget.

The limitations section acknowledges some real failure modes, including ambiguous conditioning, hallucinated semantics, and a remaining quality gap relative to stronger commercial or non-MLLM 3D systems.
weaknesses: The central claims are much stronger than the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims native/end-to-end high-fidelity 3D generation within an MLLM, but the system depends heavily on a pretrained Hunyuan3D VAE and material generator; the novelty over plugging an LLM/MoT interface into an existing 3D latent decoder is not clearly isolated.

The evaluation is under-specified and not sufficiently convincing. Dataset sizes, train/test filtering, prompt construction, rendering protocol, baseline reproduction details, and user-study design are all missing or vague, making it hard to judge fairness or reproduce the numbers.

The comparison to state-of-the-art 3D generators is weak. The proposed method is not best overall in Table 1: TRELLIS is much better on p-FID/p-KID, Hunyuan3D is better on CLIP, SAM3D is better in the user study, and the claimed advantage mainly holds only within the narrower MLLM-based subset.

The 3D understanding claim is not adequately supported. The method improves over image-only VLM baselines on caption metrics, but still trails 3D-LLM, PointLLM, and ShapeLLM-Omni; moreover, the paper admits the captions are short MLLM-generated labels, so BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR on this target are a poor proxy for genuine spatial reasoning.

The claim that 3D generation transfers back to perception lacks a proper causal ablation. There is no clean comparison between the same architecture trained with and without 3D generation under matched data, scale, and schedule.

Several ablations are too coarse to validate the design choices. The MoT, token budget, backbone size, and VAE changes are entangled with capacity and compute, while important alternatives such as simpler adapters, single-transformer variants at matched compute, and direct diffusion/AR baselines are not convincingly controlled.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper gives some optimizer and inference settings, but omits enough implementation detail, training duration, exact data composition, preprocessing scripts, evaluation code, checkpoint availability, and user-study methodology that others could not reliably reproduce the results.

The presentation has many rough edges: grammatical issues, inconsistent terminology, overbroad wording such as “true spatial intelligence,” missing spaces/formatting problems, and several assertions that read more like positioning than substantiated technical conclusions.

The ethics/impact statement is perfunctory and does not engage with relevant risks for 3D asset generation, such as dataset licensing, misuse for deceptive synthetic assets, memorization of copyrighted 3D objects, or downstream safety implications.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: bringing 3D generation and captioning into a unified MLLM-style architecture, rather than treating 3D synthesis as a separate downstream generator.

The proposed TokenAR/BlockAR mixture design is a sensible architectural adaptation for long 3D latent sequences, and the paper gives plausible motivation for separating serial token modeling from parallel block-level 3D generation.

Empirical results show clear gains over prior MLLM-based 3D generation methods on p-FID, p-KID, MUSIQ, and the user study, and the ablations support the value of the stronger 3D VAE, MoT architecture, larger token budget, and Qwen3-VL backbone.
The paper is honest that the method does not yet surpass the best non-MLLM 3D generators, and it includes useful failure cases and practical observations about AdaLN and Hunyuan3D VAE point sampling.
weaknesses: Some central claims are overstated. The method relies heavily on a frozen Hunyuan3D-2.1 VAE and its material generator, so claims of native or fully end-to-end high-fidelity 3D generation within an LLM framework need sharper qualification.

The evidence for 3D understanding transfer is limited. The captioning experiment primarily evaluates image-based rendered 3D understanding, improves over generic image VLMs, but still trails dedicated 3D-understanding models by a noticeable margin.

The evaluation is not fully convincing against the broader 3D generation state of the art: non-MLLM baselines outperform the method on important metrics such as TRELLIS p-FID/p-KID and SAM3D user preference, while the MLLM gains over ShapeLLM-Omni on p-FID/p-KID are relatively modest.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript lacks key details such as training set sizes after filtering, number of training steps, compute budget beyond GPU type/count, exact baseline evaluation protocol, user study design, prompt construction, statistical uncertainty, and whether code/checkpoints will be released.

Presentation is generally understandable but uneven, with typos, formatting issues, and several vague methodological descriptions, especially around the shared causal-parallel attention, block construction, positional scheme, and training schedule.

The impact statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully discuss potential misuse or provenance concerns for 3D asset generation, despite the use of large scraped/curated 3D datasets and generative modeling capabilities.
